The AI Chip Boom’s Uncomfortable Arithmeticby Malcolm Penn on 11-19-2026 at 8:00 am

Categories: AI, Future Horizons, Semiconductor Services

Key takeaways ▼

The semiconductor industry’s biggest risk may be misunderstanding its own success. When revenues rise dramatically, the natural response is to expand capacity, secure supplies and prepare for sustained growth. But those decisions become dangerous if higher sales reflect sharply rising prices rather than an equally strong increase in underlying demand.
That distinction makes Future Horizons’ November report significant. Its central warning concerns the composition of the AI-driven boom: how much comes from additional chips, how much from higher selling prices, and how heavily the industry depends on one concentrated source of spending.
According to the report, September semiconductor revenues increased 150 percent year on year. Yet total semiconductor unit shipments rose just 9.9 percent, while average selling prices increased 127.5 percent. Those figures describe a market whose financial expansion substantially exceeds its physical growth. For businesses planning factories, equipment purchases or supply commitments, that difference changes the calculation.
Revenue measures what customers spend. Unit demand helps explain how much production capacity they need. Confusing the two can encourage manufacturers to build for a market that looks much larger in dollars than it does in wafers or devices. If pricing subsequently weakens, the revenue supporting those investment assumptions can disappear faster than the capacity built to serve it.
Memory illustrates the exposure. Future Horizons reports memory revenue growth of 383 percent, combining a 52.4 percent increase in units with a 217 percent increase in average selling prices. Demand is clearly growing, but pricing contributes heavily to the headline result. That creates vulnerability when supply expands, purchasing patterns change or customers become less willing to absorb higher costs.
The consequences extend beyond memory manufacturers. Equipment suppliers, packaging companies and test providers all make commitments against customers’ expansion plans. Strong demand for advanced AI products can justify investment, but aggregate market growth offers limited guidance about which technologies, production stages and applications will sustain orders.
The report also highlights an uneven competitive landscape. Hyperscalers pursuing AI infrastructure can tolerate component prices that create serious difficulties for more price-sensitive applications. Smartphone and PC manufacturers face different economics. Higher memory costs can squeeze margins, force specification changes or increase retail prices, potentially weakening demand elsewhere in the electronics market.
This matters because semiconductor businesses rarely operate in isolation. A powerful AI investment cycle can coexist with fragile conditions across other customer groups. Treating headline growth as evidence of universal recovery risks overlooking those differences and allocating resources poorly.
There is also a timing problem. Semiconductor capacity takes time to develop, while customer confidence and purchasing intentions can change quickly. Companies committing capital during shortages may bring capacity online after the strongest pricing conditions have passed. Future Horizons’ downturn forecast remains a forecast, but the mismatch between investment lead times and market adjustment deserves attention regardless of its precise timing.
Its comparison between today’s AI infrastructure and the historical contest between electrical architectures raises a separate strategic question: will the technologies attracting the most capital today remain the preferred way to deliver AI tomorrow?
That analogy does not establish which architecture will win. It does underline the risk of assuming that current resource requirements will scale indefinitely. Better efficiency, different computing approaches or changes in workload economics could alter the demand for particular devices without diminishing AI’s broader importance.
For industry leaders, the practical response is more granular planning. Revenue, shipment volumes, product mix, customer concentration and capacity commitments need separate examination. Investment cases should remain credible under less favorable pricing and slower infrastructure spending.
Bottom Line: The report matters because a transformative technology can generate both durable opportunity and cyclical excess. Believing in AI’s future does not remove the need to question the economics of its present rollout. The companies best positioned for the next phase will understand what customers actually need, what they can sustainably afford and which investments remain useful when scarcity no longer supports exceptional prices. That discipline will shape resilience across the semiconductor supply chain.
